title: Greetings and introducing yourself
objectives: Greet people at any time of day and respond to Kumusta?
Use the polite particles po and opo with older people and strangers
Introduce yourself with Ako si... and say where you are from with taga-
Use the seven doer-form (ang-form) pronouns: ako, ikaw/ka, siya, kami, tayo, kayo, sila

grammar.title: The polite particles po and opo
grammar.explanation:
Tagalog has a small word, po, that adds respect to anything you say. You use it when talking to older people, strangers, customers, teachers — anyone you would call 'sir' or 'ma'am' in English. It usually sits after the first word or two of the sentence: Salamat po. Magandang umaga po.

Opo is the polite version of oo (yes). So a child answering a grandparent says opo, not oo. There is no polite version of hindi (no); you just add po: Hindi po.

When in doubt, use po. Filipinos never mind extra politeness, but leaving po out with an elder can sound rude. With friends your own age, drop it — Kumusta ka? is fine.

grammar.title: Introducing yourself: Ako si...
grammar.explanation:
To say your name, use Ako si + name: Ako si Ana — 'I am Ana'. The little word si goes in front of a person's name; think of it as a name tag that Tagalog requires. You never say just 'Ako Ana'.

To introduce someone else, point the same pattern at them: Siya si Ben — 'He/She is Ben'. Notice that siya covers both 'he' and 'she'; Tagalog pronouns do not mark gender at all.

To ask someone's name, the everyday question is Ano ang pangalan mo? — literally 'What is your name?'. Learn it as a chunk for now; the little word mo ('your') gets its full explanation in a later unit.

grammar.title: The doer-form pronouns (ang-form)
grammar.explanation:
Tagalog pronouns come in sets. The first set you need is the doer form — traditionally called the 'ang-form' because these pronouns play the same role as words marked with ang. They name the person a sentence is about: ako (I), ikaw/ka (you), siya (he/she), kami (we, not including you), tayo (we, including you), kayo (you plural, also polite singular), sila (they).

Two things trip up beginners. First, 'you' has two shapes: ikaw starts a sentence (Ikaw si Ben?), while ka goes after another word and can never be first (Kumusta ka?). Second, Tagalog splits English 'we' in two: kami excludes the listener ('we, but not you'), tayo includes them ('we, you and I'). If you invite someone along, that's tayo.

Kayo doubles as a polite singular 'you', just like French 'vous' — so a waiter asks an older customer Kumusta po kayo?

Unlike English, these pronouns usually come after the descriptive word: Mabuti ako, literally 'Fine I' = 'I am fine'. There is no word for 'am/is/are' — the pronoun and the description just sit next to each other.

grammar.title: Saying where you're from: taga- and taga-saan
grammar.explanation:
To say where you are from, stick taga- in front of the place name: taga-Maynila (from Manila), taga-Amerika (from America), taga-Cebu (from Cebu). Then add your pronoun: Taga-Maynila ako — 'I'm from Manila'.

The question is Taga-saan ka? — 'Where are you from?' (saan means 'where'). Polite version: Taga-saan po kayo?

Notice the word order again: the taga- word comes first, the pronoun second. This 'description first, doer second' order is the normal rhythm of Tagalog sentences, and you will see it constantly.

vocab.note: From Spanish 'como esta'; also spelled kamusta in casual writing
Placed after the first word or phrase of the sentence
Also negates statements: Hindi ako guro = I am not a teacher
A bit formal; friends often just say sige or ingat
ikaw starts a sentence; ka follows another word and is never first
No gender in Tagalog pronouns — siya is both 'he' and 'she'
Attaches to place names: taga-Maynila, taga-Amerika
'Titser' is also very common in speech

vocab.en: on the other hand; in turn (softener)
vocab.note: Ikaw naman? = And you? Also softens answers: Mabuti naman.
din after consonants, rin after vowels: Mabuti rin ako.
Turns a statement into a question: Estudyante ka ba?

dialogue.title: Meeting at a birthday party
dialogue.context: Ana meets Ben, a friend of the host, for the first time at a party in Quezon City.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.tl: Magandang gabi! Mabuti naman ako. Ikaw?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.tl: Ako naman si Ben. Taga-saan ka, Ana?
lines.en: And I'm Ben. Where are you from, Ana?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.en: I'm from Cebu. And you, where are you from?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.en: I'm from Manila. Are you a student?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.en: Yes, I'm a student. How about you?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.tl: Ay, guro! Siya ba si Carlos?
lines.en: Oh, a teacher! Is that Carlos?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.tl: Oo, siya si Carlos. Kaibigan ko siya.
lines.en: Yes, that's Carlos. He's my friend.

exercises.prompt: It's 8 in the morning and you greet your neighbor politely. What do you say?
exercises.explain: Umaga means morning, so the morning greeting is magandang umaga; po makes it polite.

exercises.prompt: Your friend's grandmother asks if you are a student. Which is the polite way to say yes?
exercises.explain: Opo is the polite form of oo (yes), used with elders. Plain oo would sound too casual here.

exercises.hint: The marker that goes before a person's name.
exercises.explain: Personal names always take the marker si: Ako si Maria.
Ka is the form of 'you' used after another word; it can never start a sentence, and ikaw is not used in this position.

exercises.hint: The softening particle used when answering 'how are you'.
exercises.explain: Mabuti naman ako is the standard, natural reply; naman softens the answer, like 'I'm fine, thanks'.
Taga-saan asks about origin ('from where'), and po kayo makes the question polite.

exercises.prompt: You and your friends (but NOT the person you're talking to) are from Davao. Which is correct?
exercises.explain: Kami is 'we' excluding the listener; tayo would wrongly include the person you're talking to.

exercises.prompt: Taga-Cebu ka ba? — Hindi, taga-Maynila ___. (No, I'm from Manila.)
exercises.explain: The doer pronoun ako comes after the description taga-Maynila — 'description first, doer second'.

exercises.prompt: I am Ana. I am from Cebu.
accept: Ako po si Ana. Taga-Cebu po ako
exercises.explain: Names take si (Ako si Ana), and taga- + place comes before the pronoun: Taga-Cebu ako.

exercises.tl: Magandang hapon po! Kumusta po kayo?
exercises.prompt: When and to whom is this said?
choices: In the morning, to a close friend
In the afternoon, politely to someone respected
exercises.explain: Magandang hapon is the afternoon greeting, and po + kayo signal politeness toward an elder or a person you respect.

exercises.answer: I am not a teacher. I am a student.
accept: I am not a teacher. I am a student
I'm not a teacher. I'm a student
I am not a teacher, I am a student
exercises.explain: Hindi before a description negates it: hindi ako guro = 'I am not a teacher'. No word for 'am' is needed.

exercises.prompt: You are inviting the person you're talking to: 'Let's go, we (you and I) are friends!' Which 'we' fits — Kaibigan ___?
exercises.explain: Tayo is the inclusive 'we' — it includes the listener, which is exactly what an invitation needs.
Taga- + place, then the polite po, the question particle ba, and the polite pronoun kayo.

exercises.prompt: Say 'thank you very much' politely: ___ salamat po.
exercises.explain: Maraming salamat po literally means 'many thanks (polite)' — the standard way to say thank you very much.
